mcqs.question: Why do production recommenders split into a cheap candidate-generation stage and a more expensive ranking stage instead of running one model over the whole catalog?
options: Because ranking models cannot handle categorical features
Because two-tower models are inherently more accurate than any ranking model
Because candidate generation and ranking must always be trained on completely different datasets
Because the expensive, feature-rich ranking model can only afford to run on a small shortlist, so a cheap stage first narrows millions of items down to a few hundred candidates
mcqs.explanation: The split is a latency/cost trade-off: a cheap retrieval stage keeps the expensive per-candidate ranking model's workload small enough to run in real time. Feature handling isn't the issue, the two stages typically train on related data, and two-tower models are chosen for speed, not for being more accurate than a ranker.

mcqs.question: Why is diversity typically enforced as a re-ranking step after the relevance model scores candidates, rather than built directly into the relevance model?
options: Because it's simpler and more controllable to penalize near-duplicates and inject exploration on top of a clean relevance ranking than to bake an inherently list-level property into a per-item scoring model
Because relevance models are physically incapable of processing more than one item at a time
Because diversity only matters for search systems, not recommenders
Because re-ranking is required by law for any personalization system
mcqs.explanation: Diversity is a property of the whole list, not any single item's score, so it's cleaner to apply as a re-ranking pass than to force a per-item relevance model to somehow reason about the rest of the list. The other options are simply false.

mcqs.question: Optimizing purely for click-through rate creates a clickbait feedback loop. What's the underlying cause?
options: CTR is mathematically impossible to compute accurately at scale
The training label (a click) doesn't capture whether the content was actually valuable after the click, so the model learns to maximize the easiest-to-game proxy instead of the real outcome
Click-through rate only applies to text ads, not to general recommendations
Clickbait happens only when the ranking model is underfit
mcqs.explanation: The problem is a mismatch between the optimized proxy (click) and the actual goal (value delivered) — the model faithfully learns exactly what it's told to optimize. CTR is perfectly computable, applies broadly beyond ads, and the issue isn't underfitting; a well-fit model on a bad label still produces this loop.

mcqs.question: A pointwise ranker outputs 0.15 for item A. What does this number mean if the model is well-calibrated, and why does this matter beyond just ordering candidates?
options: It approximates the actual probability a user would click item A in that position, which lets the same score feed other downstream decisions (like an ad bidding threshold), not just relative ordering
It's an arbitrary internal score with no real-world meaning beyond ranking order
It means item A is guaranteed to be the single best item in the candidate list
It represents the fraction of the training set that consisted of item A
mcqs.explanation: Calibration means the output can be read as a genuine probability estimate, which is valuable precisely because it supports decisions beyond ranking order alone, like whether a score clears some absolute threshold. It's not merely an arbitrary internal score, doesn't guarantee A is the single best item (only that its estimated click probability is 0.15), and has nothing to do with training-set composition.

mcqs.question: A recommender's ranking model is trained directly on raw click logs from the current production ranking, with no adjustment. What risk does this create?
options: None — click logs are a direct and unbiased measure of true preference
Click logs cannot be used to train ranking models at all
This risk only applies to search engines, not recommendation systems
The model partly learns to reproduce the current ranking's position advantage (items clicked because they were shown first) rather than genuine relevance, creating a self-reinforcing feedback loop
mcqs.explanation: Because position itself drives clicks independent of relevance, naive training on raw logs entangles 'ranked highly already' with 'genuinely preferred,' reinforcing whatever the current model already does. Click logs are not unbiased in this way, the same position-bias mechanism applies to recommenders just as it does to search, and click logs are absolutely usable for training, just not without correcting for this bias.
